name: Fatima Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking to me, Fatima. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head shepherd at Upper Lynd, a hill farm with 900 ewes, 60 beef cows and a few fields of oats and turnips for winter feed. Most days I'm on the quad bike by seven with my two dogs, Moss and Tib, checking the hill. In spring it's lambing, sometimes twenty hours a day, and in summer it's gathering, shearing and dipping.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being on the hill when the cloud lifts, and I like that Gareth Pryce, the farmer, trusts me with the whole flock. What wears me out is the money side. Hill farms like Upper Lynd live on government payments for looking after the land, and those rules change every few years, so my wage is never quite safe. My partner Daniel's a mechanic in Bramford, we rent a cottage in the village, and we've got maybe three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Well, I'd half expected that. Sheep don't read the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say that farming doesn't change as fast as people on screens think. At the mart I'd joke that the only robot I trust is the quad bike. I'd keep it light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means the same old worries. The government land payments are my real risk, because if those get cut, Gareth can't pay a head shepherd. AI fizzling out doesn't help or hurt that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd take on more contract shearing in June and July, which pays well per sheep. And I'd try to put a hundred a month aside after shearing season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, with a little knot about money. Same as any year, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the land payments were cut, what would Gareth do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth would probably cut the flock and do more of it himself, and he's fifty-eight with a bad knee. He'd keep me as long as he could. But if the government cuts the hill farm payments, there's no head shepherd job on Upper Lynd (the hill farm she works on).

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the contract shearing bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a good summer, maybe two thousand. That's our holiday, our car tax and the boiler service. Without shearing, Daniel and I would be in trouble by September.

say: I'd say farming **changes slower** than people on screens think.
I'd joke at the mart that the only robot I trust is the **quad bike**.
think: The real risk is **government land payments**, not AI.
If those get cut, Gareth **can't pay** a head shepherd.
do: Carry on with the **hill flock** as now.
Take on more **contract shearing** in June and July.
Put **a hundred a month** aside after shearing season.
feel: **Steady**, with a little knot about money.
S0.quote: If the government cuts the hill farm payments, there's no head shepherd job on Upper Lynd (the hill farm she works on).
fieldNote: Her wage depends on **government payments**, which she sees as the real threat.
**Contract shearing** money is essential to the household budget.
She is **calm in tone** but money is always present.

steps.text: Keep shepherding the 900 ewes on Upper Lynd as now
Book extra contract shearing jobs in June and July
Set aside a hundred a month after shearing season

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds likely. It's already creeping in at the mart office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the paperwork side will get easier and the hill won't change much. That's mostly what I'd say, at the mart and to friends. I'm not one for posting opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it helps me more than it hurts. I already use the chat AI now and then to fill in the land payment forms, which used to take Gareth and me a whole weekend. The bit I'd watch is Daniel, because garages are going to AI for diagnosing faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn to use AI properly for the flock records and payment forms, once a couple of farms near us had it working. I'd keep the shearing going. And I'd talk to Daniel about whether his garage is planning anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly for Daniel. I'm fine with the change if it means less paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change for Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel says the diagnostic computer already does half the thinking. If AI does the rest, the garage might need fewer mechanics, or pay them less. Daniel's good with his hands, so I think he'd stay, but I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for other farms first. Which ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our neighbours are always first with new kit. If the Hendersons (her neighbours) at Low Cragg have used new kit through a lambing without it falling over, I'll try it. I'm not paying to be the test farm.

say: I'd say the **paperwork** gets easier and the hill **won't change** much.
I'd say that at the mart, but I'm **not one for posting** opinions.
think: It **helps me** more than it hurts, by cutting form-filling.
**Daniel's garage** may need fewer mechanics as AI does diagnosis.
do: Learn AI for **flock records** and payment forms once nearby farms use it.
Talk with Daniel about his **garage's plans**.
S1.quote: If the Hendersons (her neighbours) at Low Cragg have used new kit through a lambing without it falling over, I'll try it.
fieldNote: She sees thinking AI as **useful** for her paperwork-heavy hill farm.
Her worry shifts to **Daniel's job** at the garage.
She follows the **early adopters** nearby before trying tools.

steps.text: Use AI for flock records and land payment forms after Low Cragg does

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. And robots by 2031. That's very soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for country areas, because they always get forgotten. I'd say it at the mart and maybe to the local councillor. I wouldn't shout about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think hill farms might be among the last to get robots, simply because Gareth couldn't afford one on our margins. But a big buyer could take over Upper Lynd and plant it with trees, and then there's no shepherd needed at all. And Daniel's garage would be in trouble by 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd save every spare penny, and we'd stop looking at buying a house. I'd learn to fly a drone for checking the hill, because that's the bit of robot work I could own. And I'd push Daniel to look at farm machinery repairs, which feel safer than cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not panic, but I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the three years between the AI and the robots. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hill keeps me for three more years while my partner's garage goes first. That's backwards from how I'd like it. I'd be the earner, which I've never been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Daniel say to each other that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Daniel we're not buying a house yet, and that we'll be fine for a while on what I bring in. He'd say he's not living off his girlfriend's sheep money. We'd laugh, then we wouldn't.

say: I'd say country areas need a **plan**, because they get forgotten.
I'd raise it with the **local councillor**, quietly.
think: Hill farms may be **among the last** to get robots, due to margins.
A buyer could **plant Upper Lynd** with trees and need no shepherd.
**Daniel's garage** would be in trouble by 2028.
do: Save **every spare penny** and stop house hunting.
Learn to fly a **drone** for checking the hill.
S2.quote: The hill keeps me for three more years while my partner's garage goes first.
fieldNote: The AI-then-robots gap means **Daniel's job goes first**, reversing their household roles.
She thinks **cost**, not ability, would keep robots off the hill.
A **forestry buyer** is her biggest outside threat.

steps.text: Save every spare penny from wages and shearing
Put off buying a house with Daniel
Learn to fly a drone for checking sheep on the hill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots around 2034. That's still quick, but you've got a bit of road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get country areas ready, if people stop talking and start doing. I'd say that to the farmers' union rep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives Daniel and me time to sort ourselves out. I could get a drone licence and do sheep gathering for other farms. I still think Upper Lynd's future depends on who owns it, not on robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a drone pilot licence in the first year. Then I'd offer drone gathering and flock counts to farms around us, maybe eighty a day. And we'd keep saving for a house but buy later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steadier. I'd have something to work on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI for planning the drone business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, now and then, for quotes and route plans. I'd let it do the dull bits. I wouldn't let it decide which sheep need a closer look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Moss and Tib in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Moss and Tib would still come out with me, because a drone can find sheep but it can't move them through a gate. A good dog is worth more than any drone on a wet day. I'd keep them as long as they can run.

say: I'd say there's time to get **country areas** ready if people start doing.
I'd tell that to the **union rep**.
think: Five years gives Daniel and me **time to sort** ourselves out.
Upper Lynd's future depends on **who owns it**, not on robots.
do: Get a **drone pilot licence** in the first year.
Offer **drone gathering** and flock counts for about eighty a day.
Keep saving for a house but **buy later**.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier, with something to work on.
S3.quote: A good dog is worth more than any drone on a wet day.
fieldNote: More time lets her build a **drone side business**.
She'd use AI for **dull tasks only**, keeping judgment for herself.
Her **sheepdogs** symbolise skills she thinks machines can't match yet.

steps.text: Get a drone pilot licence in the first year
Sell drone sheep gathering and counts to nearby farms
Keep saving for a house deposit with Daniel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a lot of lambings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this right, so no excuses. I'd say it to the union rep and at the mart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. I'd have time to build up my own small flock on rented grazing, and the drone work. If I own something, I'm not just waiting on Gareth's (her boss's) decisions or the government's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the first few years I'd buy fifty ewes and rent grazing from the Hendersons. I'd get the drone licence when the kit is cheaper. And Daniel and I would start properly saving for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can handle. It's like looking at a long winter with a full hay barn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fifty ewes is a risk with thin savings. How would you pay for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small loan from the farmers' credit union, and the shearing money. If it goes wrong, I sell them back at the mart. Sheep are about the easiest thing in the world to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gareth about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Gareth I'm not leaving, I just want my own flock too. Gareth started with forty ewes himself. He'd probably give me a talk about grass and wish me luck.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this **right**.
I'd say **no excuses** at the mart and to the union rep.
think: I'd be **all right**, with time to build my own flock.
If I **own something**, I'm not just waiting on others.
do: Buy **fifty ewes** and rent grazing from the Hendersons.
Get the **drone licence** once kit is cheaper.
Start saving with Daniel for a **house**.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to handle it, like a winter with a full hay barn.
S4.quote: If I own something, I'm not just waiting on Gareth's (her boss's) decisions or the government's.
fieldNote: With ten years she moves toward **ownership**: her own small flock.
She finances it with **credit union** debt, a careful risk.
Her **relationship with Gareth** stays warm and respectful.

steps.text: Buy fifty ewes with a credit union loan and rent Henderson grazing
Get a drone pilot licence once the kit is cheaper
Save each month with Daniel for a house

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Daniel's job could go first and we'd have nothing behind us. What would help is keeping the hill farm payments steady, and cheap training for things like drone licences. Rural places need help that actually reaches them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who looks after the hill if no one's farming it. Upper Lynd isn't just sheep, it's walls, drains and footpaths. If the shepherds go, nobody fixes the walls on the hill.

headlineQuote: If the shepherds go, nobody fixes the walls on the hill.
portrait: Fatima, 27, is **head shepherd** on a hill farm, working 900 ewes with her two dogs.
She and Daniel, a mechanic, have about **three weeks** of savings and rent a village cottage.
Her wage depends on **government land payments**, which she sees as her main risk.
She tries tools once **neighbours prove them**, and plans a drone gathering business.
She worries most when **Daniel's garage** is hit first, and is uneasy to anxious throughout.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Daniel's job could go first and they'd have nothing behind them.
whatWouldHelp: Steady **hill farm payments** from the government.
Cheap training like **drone licences** that reaches rural areas.
